title: The martyrdom of St. Henry Morse
shortBlurb: Hanged at Tyburn after three banishments and four imprisonments, the plague-year priest of London gave his life for the Catholic mission to England…
body: On 1 February 1645, by the new reckoning — England still called the year 1644 — Henry Morse, a priest of the Society of Jesus, was hanged, drawn, and quartered at Tyburn under the statute that made his priesthood treason. Born at Brome in Suffolk in 1595 and bred to the law, he had been received into the Church as a young man, trained at Douai and at the English College at Rome, and ordained in 1625.

He labored first in the north of England, and made his Jesuit novitiate behind prison walls. In London during the plague years of 1636 and 1637 he ministered to the sick beside St. John Southworth, himself falling ill yet returning to his stricken flock. Thrice banished and four times imprisoned, he was seized at last in Cumberland amid the Civil War and brought to the capital for trial.
At the gallows he forgave his enemies and professed that he died for the faith alone. In 1970 Pope Paul VI canonized him among the Forty Martyrs of England and Wales.

title: The death of St. Ansgar, Apostle of the North
shortBlurb: The Apostle of the North died at Bremen after forty years of patient mission among the Danes and the Swedes…
body: On 3 February 865 St. Ansgar died at Bremen, aged about sixty-three. Born near Amiens in 801 and a monk of Corbie and then of Corvey, he was sent by the Emperor Louis the Pious to preach to the Danes in 826, and about the years 829 to 831 he sowed the faith at Birka in Sweden.

Consecrated about 831 the first archbishop of Hamburg, with a mandate to bring Christianity to the northern peoples, he saw his city burned by Viking pirates in 845; about 849 the see of Bremen was joined to his charge, and from there he patiently rebuilt his ruined mission, ransoming captives, founding churches, and winning the confidence of kings.

His disciple and successor Rimbert wrote the Vita Anskarii, the chief record of his life, which praises his prayer and his humility above his miracles. He is honored as the Enlightener of Denmark and Sweden, and the Church keeps his feast on the day of his death.

sources.text: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii (tr. Robinson, Anskar: The Apostle of the North, 1921; public domain)

title: The Twenty-Six Martyrs of Japan
shortBlurb: On a hill above Nagasaki, twenty-six missionaries and Japanese faithful were crucified rather than renounce Christ…
body: On 5 February 1597, on the hill of Nishizaka overlooking Nagasaki, twenty-six Christians were raised on crosses and pierced with spears: six Franciscan missionaries — Spaniards, a Portuguese, and the Mexican-born Felipe de Jesús — three Japanese Jesuits, Paul Miki, John Goto, and James Kisai, and seventeen Japanese lay Franciscans, among them three boys, the youngest twelve years old.

Seized at Kyoto and Osaka by order of the ruler Toyotomi Hideyoshi, who since 1587 had forbidden the missionaries, they had their ears cropped and were marched some five hundred miles through the winter to the place of execution, that their death might terrify the most Christian city of Japan.

From his cross Paul Miki preached his last sermon, forgiving his persecutors and confessing that there is no way to salvation but the Christian way. The martyrs were beatified by Urban VIII in 1627 and canonized by Pius IX in 1862; the universal Church keeps their memory on 6 February, but Japan honors them on the day of their triumph.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “Sts. Peter Baptist and Twenty-Five Companions”

title: The election of Pope Pius XI
shortBlurb: A librarian from Milan became pope and blessed the world from the loggia no pope had used since 1870…
body: On 6 February 1922, on the fourteenth ballot of the conclave that had opened four days before after the death of Benedict XV, Cardinal Achille Ratti, Archbishop of Milan, was elected pope and took the name Pius XI. Born at Desio in 1857, he had been prefect of the Ambrosian Library in Milan and then of the Vatican Library, nuncio to the reborn Poland, and a cardinal only since the previous June.

His first act was a sign read round the world: he gave the blessing Urbi et Orbi from the outer loggia of St. Peter's, which no pope had used since the loss of Rome in 1870, as if to say the self-imposed imprisonment of the Vatican would not last. Seven years later he sealed the Lateran Pacts.
His seventeen-year pontificate gave the Church the encyclicals Quadragesimo anno and Mit brennender Sorge, the feast of Christ the King, Vatican Radio, and a long roll of canonizations.

sources.text: Vatican biography of Pope Pius XI (vatican.va)

title: St. Athanasius flees into the desert
shortBlurb: When soldiers broke into the church of St. Theonas at the night vigil, the champion of Nicaea vanished into the desert…
body: In the night of 8 February 356, while St. Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria since 328, kept a vigil with his people in the church of St. Theonas, the troops of the general Syrianus surrounded the building — more than five thousand men, the historians reckon — broke down the doors, and pressed up the nave with arrows flying.

The bishop sat upon his throne and bade the deacon intone Psalm 136, that the people might answer “for his mercy endureth for ever”; he would not stir until his flock had escaped, and then his clergy hurried him, half fainting, through the tumult. He was carried to safety among the monks of the desert, who hid him for six years and never betrayed him.

It was his third exile for the Nicene faith. The intruded George of Cappadocia took the see, but Athanasius returned under Julian in 362, outlived the enmity of four emperors, and died in 373, the unbowed confessor of the divinity of the Son.

sources.text: Gwatkin, The Arian Controversy (1914; public domain)

title: The execution of Mary Queen of Scots
shortBlurb: Condemned for the Babington plot, the captive queen went to the block at Fotheringhay professing the Catholic faith…
body: On the morning of 8 February 1587 Mary Stuart, Queen of Scots, was beheaded in the great hall of Fotheringhay Castle, after nineteen years of captivity in England. A commission of thirty-six noblemen had condemned her the previous October for complicity in the Babington plot against Queen Elizabeth, whose death warrant was signed on 1 February.

She went to the block as to a sacrifice, bearing a crucifix and a Latin book of hours; denied her chaplain, she prayed aloud in Latin and in English, forgave her enemies, and declared that she died a true Catholic. In her last letter, written six hours before to the King of France, she named as the cause of her death “the Catholic faith and the assertion of my God-given right to the English crown.”

Catholic Europe mourned her as a martyr of the faith, and her death hardened the counsels that sent the Spanish Armada the following year. Buried first at Peterborough, she was translated in 1612 by her son, King James I, to a royal tomb in Westminster Abbey.

title: St. John Vianney is sent to Ars
shortBlurb: A peasant's son who had failed his examinations was sent to a forgotten village and made it the confessional of France…
body: On 9 February 1818, a few weeks after the death of his mentor the Abbé Balley, the young priest Jean-Baptiste-Marie Vianney was appointed parish priest of Ars, a hamlet of some two hundred and thirty souls in the Dombes, north of Lyon, whose faith had grown cold since the Revolution.

Born at Dardilly in 1786 and ordained in 1815 after long struggles with Latin, he found the village so little known that, the story runs, he lost his way to it and was set right by a boy minding sheep. For more than forty years he prayed, fasted, preached against dancing and blasphemy, and reconciled sinners to God.

Ars became a place of pilgrimage: by the 1850s tens of thousands came every year, and the curé spent as many as sixteen hours a day in the confessional. He died in 1859, was canonized in 1925, and is the patron of parish priests throughout the world.

title: The death of Pope Pius XI
shortBlurb: The pope of the Lateran Pacts died on the eve of an address he meant to raise against the racial laws…
body: On 10 February 1939 Pope Pius XI died in the Vatican, aged eighty-one, on the eve of the day appointed for an address to the bishops of Italy gathered for the tenth anniversary of the Lateran Pacts — an address, it was said, in which he meant to speak plainly against the racial laws then spreading in Europe.

Born Ambrogio Damiano Achille Ratti at Desio in 1857 and elected in 1922, he had reigned seventeen years: he settled the Roman Question in 1929, wrote Quadragesimo anno and Mit brennender Sorge, instituted the feast of Christ the King, founded Vatican Radio, and canonized St. Thomas More and St. John Fisher together in 1935.

He was buried in the grottoes of St. Peter's, and on 2 March the cardinals chose in his place his Secretary of State, Eugenio Pacelli, who took the name Pius XII — a succession that opened on the very brink of the Second World War.

sources.text: Vatican biography of Pope Pius XI (vatican.va)

title: The birth of Vatican Radio
shortBlurb: Marconi built it, and a pope's voice went out for the first time to all peoples and every creature…
body: On 12 February 1931 Pope Pius XI inaugurated the Vatican Radio, the Statio Radiophonica Vaticana, built for the Holy See within the Vatican Gardens by Guglielmo Marconi, the pioneer of wireless telegraphy, and blessed the instruments that were to carry the apostolic word to peoples far away.

The first voice carried on its waves was Marconi's, announcing that the Pope's voice could now be heard “simultaneously over the entire surface of the earth”; then Pius XI himself spoke in Latin, in the message Qui arcano Dei, opening with the words of Isaiah, “Hear, O islands, and listen, O distant peoples,” and addressing “all peoples and every creature” — the first broadcast of a pope in history.

From that day the Pope's Radio has carried the Gospel, the teaching of the successors of Peter, and the news of the Church to every continent, in more than forty languages; it stands today at the heart of Vatican News, ninety-five years on.

sources.text: Vatican, “February 12, 1931, the day Vatican Radio was born” (comunicazione.va)

title: Galileo arrives in Rome to face the Inquisition
shortBlurb: Old and ailing, the astronomer reached Rome to answer for the Dialogue before the Inquisition…
body: On 13 February 1633 Galileo Galilei, in his sixty-ninth year and in poor health, reached Rome to stand trial before the Roman Inquisition, and was lodged as the guest of Francesco Niccolini, the Grand Duke's ambassador, at the Villa Medici.

Summoned the previous October after the publication of his Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems, he had pleaded age and infirmity; but Urban VIII was inexorable, threatening to have him brought in chains, and on 20 January the old man set out from Florence upon the weary journey.

The trial opened in April, and on 22 June he knelt in Santa Maria sopra Minerva and abjured the Copernican opinion, passing the rest of his life under guard at Arcetri, where he died in 1642. The Church has since acknowledged the wrong of his condemnation; a commission appointed by John Paul II closed its work in 1992.

title: The bull Pie postulatio voluntatis
shortBlurb: Paschal II's bull made the Hospitallers of St. John an order under the Church's own protection…
body: On 15 February 1113 Pope Paschal II issued the bull Pie postulatio voluntatis, taking the hospital of St. John in Jerusalem and its brethren under the protection of the Apostolic See, and granting them the right to choose their own superiors — the founding charter of the Order known in later ages as the Knights of Malta.

The fraternity had grown from a hospice founded by merchants of Amalfi about the year 1048, near the church of the Holy Sepulchre, to care for poor and sick pilgrims; under its first master, the Blessed Gerard, it had nursed the suffering through the siege of Jerusalem in 1099.

The original bull is treasured to this day in the National Library of Malta at Valletta. In February 2013, nine hundred years on, Benedict XVI received the knights in St. Peter's and praised nine centuries of fidelity to the Church and to “our lords the sick.”

sources.text: Benedict XVI, Address to the Order of Malta for the 900th anniversary of Pie postulatio voluntatis, 9 February 2013 (vatican.va)

title: The martyrdom of St. Juliana
shortBlurb: The martyrologies keep her name at Cumae on this day, and Gregory the Great himself sent her relics…
body: Ancient tradition holds that St. Juliana was martyred about the year 304, in the persecution of Diocletian. The Martyrologium Hieronymianum keeps her memory on 16 February at Cumae, in Campania, and both the Latin and the Greek churches honor her name.

That her cult is old is certain: St. Gregory the Great, writing to Fortunatus, bishop of Naples, granted the matron Januaria's request for relics of St. Juliana for the consecration of a church on her estate. Her later acts are legend — that she was a maiden of Nicomedia who refused a heathen bridegroom, was cruelly tortured, and at last beheaded — but the veneration is genuine, and older than the story.

Her relics were treasured near Naples, and her patronage spread through the West; painters loved to show her triumph over the dragon, and the Church still names her among the virgins and martyrs of the age of persecution.

title: The burning of Giordano Bruno
shortBlurb: The philosopher of infinite worlds was burned in the Campo de' Fiori after eight years in the Inquisition's prisons…
body: On 17 February 1600 Giordano Bruno of Nola, a former Dominican friar aged fifty-two, was burned alive in the Campo de' Fiori at Rome, delivered by the Roman Inquisition to the secular arm after some eight years in its prisons.

Denounced at Venice in 1592 by his host Giovanni Mocenigo and transferred to Rome the next year, he was tried for heresies touching the faith and would not abjure. He had wandered through Europe teaching a philosophy of infinite worlds; condemned under Pope Clement VIII, he heard the sentence — tradition preserves his answer — warning his judges that perhaps they pronounced it with more fear than he received it.

In 1889 a statue was raised upon the spot, and Bruno became an emblem of free thought. The Church of our day still judges his doctrines erroneous, yet a spokesman of the Holy See has called his death a sad episode and a matter of deep regret.

title: The death of Fra Angelico
shortBlurb: The angelic friar who painted to preach died at the Minerva and lies there still…
body: On 18 February 1455 the Dominican painter Fra Giovanni da Fiesole, whom the world calls Fra Angelico, died at the convent of Santa Maria sopra Minerva in Rome, and was buried there, where his tomb is still shown.

Born Guido di Pietro at Vicchio near Florence about 1395, he entered the Order of Preachers at Fiesole and took up the brush to preach: the Annunciation and the cells of San Marco in Florence, the San Marco altarpiece, and the chapel of Pope Nicholas V in the Vatican are his. Vasari hands down that, offered the archbishopric of Florence, he begged the pope to give it to Fra Antonino instead.

Beatified by John Paul II in 1982 and named patron of artists, he is honored on the day of his death — the “angelic friar,” who, his brethren said, never took up his pencil without first falling to his knees in prayer.

title: The death of Martin Luther
shortBlurb: The reformer died in the town of his birth, leaving a Bible in German and a Christendom divided…
body: In the early morning of 18 February 1546 Martin Luther died at Eisleben, the town of his birth, whither he had journeyed in January to arbitrate a quarrel of the counts of Mansfeld. He was sixty-two, had preached for the last time four days before, and his friend Justus Jonas was among the watchers at his bedside.

Born in 1483, an Augustinian friar ordained in 1507 and doctor of theology at Wittenberg, he had set the world alight with the Ninety-Five Theses of 1517, stood before the emperor at Worms in 1521, and in 1525 married the former nun Katharina von Bora, the mother of his six children. He died excommunicate, the author of a German Bible and of a reform that split Western Christendom.

His last scribbled note ended with the words “We are beggars, that is true.” The body was borne to Wittenberg and laid in the Castle Church on 22 February; his teaching lives on in the churches that bear his name.

title: The Treaty of Tolentino
shortBlurb: Bonaparte spared Rome, and the Pope paid with Avignon, the Legations, and thirty million francs…
body: On 19 February 1797, at Tolentino in the Marches, Pope Pius VI signed a treaty of peace with General Bonaparte. The Pope had broken the armistice of Foligno, and the French army, fresh from Rivoli and the fall of Mantua, had swept the papal troops aside and stood within reach of Rome.

The price of peace was heavy: the Pope renounced Avignon and the Venaissin, annexed by France in 1791, ceded the Legations of Bologna, Ferrara, and the Romagna, and promised thirty million francs for the Directory — besides the pictures, statues, and manuscripts already exacted by the armistice of Bologna.

It bought the papacy a year's respite. When a French general was killed in a Roman riot, the Directory answered with occupation: in February 1798 a Roman Republic was proclaimed in the city, and Pius VI, an old man, was carried into exile, dying at Valence on 29 August 1799.

title: The death of Pope Julius II
shortBlurb: The warrior pope who laid the cornerstone of St. Peter's and set Michelangelo to work is dead…
body: In the night of 20-21 February 1513 Pope Julius II died in Rome, in his seventieth year. Born Giuliano della Rovere at Albisola in 1443, a nephew of Sixtus IV, he had been elected on 1 November 1503 and reigned as the warrior pope, restoring the States of the Church by arms and by craft.

He expelled the Bentivogli from Bologna in 1506, humbled Venice by the League of Cambrai, turned the Holy League against France, and in 1512 opened the Fifth Lateran Council. He laid the cornerstone of the new St. Peter's in 1506, set Michelangelo to the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel and Raphael to the Stanze, and founded the Swiss Guard.
Michelangelo's Moses, carved for the tomb Julius had planned, still watches over him at San Pietro in Vincoli. On 9 March Giovanni de' Medici succeeded him, taking the name Leo X.

title: The Battle of Benevento
shortBlurb: On the Calore plain Manfred of Hohenstaufen fell, and the Guelph cause triumphed with Charles of Anjou…
body: On 26 February 1266, on the plain of the Calore beside Benevento, Charles of Anjou, count of Provence and brother of St. Louis IX, defeated the army of Manfred, King of Sicily, the bastard son of the Emperor Frederick II, who fell fighting on the field.

The popes Urban IV and Clement IV, long at war with the house of Hohenstaufen, had called Charles into Italy and invested him with the Sicilian crown; anointed at Rome on the Epiphany of 1266, he marched south, crossed the Garigliano by the treachery of Manfred's allies, and in one bloody afternoon broke the power of Frederick's heirs.

Dante met Manfred's soul at the gate of Purgatory, buried under a cairn of stones — before the Church had his bones cast out of her lands. Two years later, on 23 August 1268 at Tagliacozzo, Charles crushed Conradin, the last of the Hohenstaufen, and the Angevin ruled in Naples.

title: The resignation of Benedict XVI takes effect
shortBlurb: At eight in the evening the first papal resignation in six centuries took effect, and the See of Peter fell vacant…
body: At eight o'clock in the evening of 28 February 2013 the resignation of Pope Benedict XVI took effect, and the Apostolic See fell vacant. He had declared it seventeen days before, on 11 February, in Latin, before the cardinals in consistory, pleading his failing strength of mind and body.

That last morning he took leave of the College of Cardinals in the Clementine Hall, then flew by helicopter to Castel Gandolfo, telling the crowd from the balcony that he would soon be “simply a pilgrim beginning the last leg of his pilgrimage on this earth.” At eight the Swiss Guard closed the doors of the palace and stood down.

No pope had laid down the office since Gregory XII in 1415, and none freely since St. Celestine V in 1294. The conclave that followed elected Pope Francis on 13 March; Benedict lived on in prayer at the Mater Ecclesiae monastery in the Vatican until his death on 31 December 2022.

title: The death of Pope St. Hilarius
shortBlurb: Leo the Great's legate at the Robber Synod ended his days on a leap day, and was buried by St. Lawrence…
body: Pope St. Hilarius died on 29 February 468 — a leap day — after six years, three months, and ten days upon the chair of Peter; some martyrologies place his death on 28 February, the day of his feast.

A Sardinian by birth and the trusted archdeacon of St. Leo the Great, he had been Leo's legate at the Second Council of Ephesus in 449 — the Robber Synod — where alone he protested the condemnation of Flavian and barely escaped the violence of Dioscorus' party; in thanksgiving he afterwards built at the Lateran the oratories of St. John the Baptist and St. John the Evangelist.

As pope he confirmed the faith of Chalcedon, corrected abuses in the churches of Gaul and Spain, and held in 465 the oldest Roman synod whose acts survive; he built libraries and a chapel of the Holy Cross by the Lateran, and was buried in the basilica of St. Lawrence-outside-the-Walls.

sources.text: Liber Pontificalis (tr. Loomis, The Book of the Popes, 1916; public domain)
